questions.question: Which button design looks more like a call-to-action rather than a text block?
questions.subtitle: Select the option that best fits the question.
questions.explanation: Effective CTAs use short, scannable, action-oriented labels. 'Deploy Vehicle' is concise and immediately clear, while 'Initiate autonomous control sequence' reads like a paragraph.

questions.question: Which layout demonstrates better visual hierarchy?
questions.subtitle: Select the option that best fits your style.
questions.explanation: Visual hierarchy guides the eye through content using size, weight, and spacing differences. Distinct heading, subheading, and body scales help users quickly find key information.

questions.question: Which pricing card has better color contrast and readability?
questions.subtitle: Select the option that best fits your style.
questions.explanationforA: Correct. Dark text on a white card passes contrast standards, the price commands attention, and the solid blue button is unmissable. Strong contrast isn't just aesthetics — it's what makes content legible for everyone, in any lighting.
questions.explanationforB: Not quite. The color's text isn't consistent text and white-on-pale-yellow may look "soft", but it strains to read and would fail accessibility contrast guidelines. The high-contrast card is stronger because readability always beats subtleness.

questions.question: Which form provides better error feedback to the user?
questions.subtitle: Select the option that best fits your style.
questions.explanationforA: Correct. This form marks exactly which fields failed and says how to fix each one — plus confirms the valid field with a check. Good error feedback locates the problem and states the fix, so users recover without hunting.
questions.explanationforB: Not quite. 'Something went wrong. Try again.' tells the user nothing — not which field failed or what to change, forcing trial and error. The inline version wins because errors sit next to the exact field with a specific fix.

questions.question: Which navigation pattern is more appropriate for desktop?
questions.subtitle: Select the option that best fits your style.
questions.explanation: On desktop, there is ample screen real estate for visible navigation links. Hiding links behind a hamburger menu reduces discoverability and adds an unnecessary extra click for users.

questions.question: Which layout uses whitespace more effectively?
questions.subtitle: Select the option that best fits your style.
questions.explanation: Whitespace (negative space) improves readability, focuses attention, and creates a sense of elegance. Cramped layouts overwhelm users and make content harder to scan.

questions.question: Which product card design is more engaging and scannable?
questions.subtitle: Select the option that best fits your style.
questions.explanationforA: Correct. Big image, bold price, star rating, stock badge, clear 'Add to cart' — every key fact lands in a two-second scan, in the order shoppers look for it. Scannable cards use hierarchy so users never have to read to decide.
questions.explanationforB: Not quite. This card hides the price inside a wall of text and offers no clear action — users must read to find what a glance should give them. The visual card wins because it surfaces image, price, and CTA through hierarchy instead of prose.

questions.question: Which design uses typography more effectively for readability?
questions.subtitle: Select the option that best fits your style.
questions.explanation: Clean, readable sans-serif fonts with proper typographic scale (distinct heading, body, and caption sizes) ensure comfortable reading. Consistent type choices build visual rhythm and trust.
